==Problem==
Al, Bill, and Cal will each randomly be assigned a whole number from <math>1</math> to <math>10</math>, inclusive, with no two of them getting the same number. What is the probability that Al's number will be a whole number multiple of Bill's and Bill's number will be a whole number multiple of Cal's?

<math>\textbf{(A) } \dfrac{9}{1000} \qquad\textbf{(B) } \dfrac{1}{90} \qquad\textbf{(C) } \dfrac{1}{80} \qquad\textbf{(D) } \dfrac{1}{72} \qquad\textbf{(E) } \dfrac{2}{121} </math>

==Video Solution==

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vulB2z_PdRE&feature=youtu.be

==Solution==
We can solve this problem with a brute force approach.

*If Cal's number is <imath>1</imath>:
**If Bill's number is <imath>2</imath>, Al's can be any of <imath>4, 6, 8, 10</imath>.
**If Bill's number is <imath>3</imath>, Al's can be any of <imath>6, 9</imath>.
**If Bill's number is <imath>4</imath>, Al's can be <imath>8</imath>.
**If Bill's number is <imath>5</imath>, Al's can be <imath>10</imath>.
**Otherwise, Al's number could not be a whole number multiple of Bill's.
*If Cal's number is <imath>2</imath>:
**If Bill's number is <imath>4</imath>, Al's can be <imath>8</imath>.
**Otherwise, Al's number could not be a whole number multiple of Bill's while Bill's number is still a whole number multiple of Cal's.
*Otherwise, Bill's number must be greater than <imath>5</imath>, i.e. Al's number could not be a whole number multiple of Bill's.

Clearly, there are exactly <imath>9</imath> cases where Al's number will be a whole number multiple of Bill's and Bill's number will be a whole number multiple of Cal's. Since there are <imath>10\cdot9\cdot8</imath> possible permutations of the numbers Al, Bill, and Cal were assigned, the probability that this is true is <imath>\frac9{10\cdot9\cdot8}=\boxed{\text{(\textbf C) }\frac1{80}}</imath>
